## Research paper

External validation and comparison of the AHA-PREVENT and pooled cohort equations for 10-year ASCVD risk prediction in a contemporary US EHR population☆

Aniket Zinzuwadia a,*, Chunying Li a, Zareen Farukhi a,b, Franco Giulianini a, Brian Cade a, Lin Chen a, Elizabeth Karlson a, Nina Paynter a, Samia Mora a,**,1, Olga Demler a,c,**,1

a Brigham & Women's Hospital, United States of America b Massachusetts General Hospital, United States of America c ETH Zurich, Switzerland

In 2023, the AHA developed new risk equations for predicting car­ diovascular risk in primary prevention. The PREVENT equations aimed to improve ASCVD risk assessment by replacing PCE, addressing PCE's miscalibration in contemporary cohorts, and removing race from the equations [1]. Overall, PREVENT generally produced lower risk esti­ mates than PCE and could significantly reduce the number of statineligible patients [2]. Here, we compared the performance of PREVENT and PCE by evaluating predicted versus observed 10-year ASCVD out­ comes across risk strata in a contemporary Massachusetts EHR cohort.

We analyzed retrospective data from the Mass General Brigham Research Patient Data Registry, an EHR repository from Boston hospi­ tals. Patients with prior ASCVD events (myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, or cardiovascular death) or statin use during 1997–2006 were excluded. Incident ASCVD events over the next 10 years (2007–2016) were identified using machine learning pheno­ types, ICD codes, and death records from the Massachusetts Department of Public Health and National Death Index. The study included 63,291 patients aged 55–79 in 2007 with complete data for calculating PRE­ VENT and PCE scores. Risk was estimated using the base PREVENT and race-specific PCE equations. Observed ASCVD event rate in the overall cohort was determined via Kaplan-Meier analysis. Risk reclassification tables were reported across PCE-based risk categories (low: <5 %, borderline: 5–7.5 %, intermediate: 7.5–20 %, high: >20 %) with abso­ lute event numbers in each stratum [3]. The study was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board.

In this cohort of 63,291 patients, the average age was 64.2 years (SD 6.8), and 38.2 % were men (Table 1). 10-year observed ASCVD event rate was 6.6 % (95 % CI: 6.4 %–6.6 %). Median predicted risks were 5.7 % (PREVENT) and 10.1 % (PCE). Using PCE and PREVENT models for

Using the 7.5 % threshold for statin eligibility, 61.1 % and 36.7 % were eligible by PCE and PREVENT, respectively. At a hypothetical 5 % threshold, eligibility was 74.2 % for PCE versus 56.7 % for PREVENT. Notably, comparing predicted to observed risk, PREVENT matched outcomes in 9 of 10 groups with >100 patients, while PCE matched in only 1 of 10 groups (Table 2).

Study limitations include adjudication of non-fatal events in a sub­ sample and underreporting of statin use by practitioners from a different hospital system. However, these biases likely affect PCE and PREVENT similarly and do not impact the primary finding of lower statin eligibility with PREVENT. To minimize informed presence bias, we restricted analysis to patients with high EHR completeness scores, used validated disease phenotypes, and incorporated death data from two govern­ mental sources [4,5]. To address variations in the timing of risk factor measurements, we used the data points nearest to 2007 to calculate 10- year risk for the 2007–2016 period.

To our knowledge, we present the first external validation study comparing PCE and PREVENT predicted risk against observed event rates within risk strata. Among a contemporary U.S. population, PRE­ VENT more accurately predicted 10-year ASCVD outcomes and reclas­ sified patients into lower-risk groups. These findings support the use of PREVENT for primary prevention, though implications of reduced statin eligibility require further discussion [6].
